zone: Tiffany Mountain north face — Tiffany Springs, Tiffany Lake and Honeymoon Pass
_areas_note: THIS IS A NORTH-SIDE FILE AND THE DISTINCTION IS THE WHOLE POINT. Tiffany Mountain is an 8,242 ft Okanogan summit whose walk-up is the Freezeout Ridge trail from a roadhead at around 6,600 ft — under three miles and less than two thousand feet, a half-day hike, and the reason the eastern Pasayten file removed this peak from its list and said it needed a Freezeout Ridge entry of its own. The NORTH FACE is a different objective reached from a different side. It is a broken six-hundred-and-fifty-foot wall of granite cut by couloirs and aretes, carrying a six-pitch route to 5.8 on the tower at its right-hand end, a five-pitch fourth-class arete, and a north-east couloir climbed as a three-pitch snow and ice line — a genuine small alpine face, not a wayside crag, whatever the area type says. Parties climbing it park at TIFFANY SPRINGS CAMPGROUND at about 6,760 ft and walk Trail 373 east past Tiffany Lake to HONEYMOON PASS at around 7,150 ft, roughly three quarters of an hour, and drop to the base from there. Nothing in this file is duplicated from any other: no zone file covers Tiffany Springs, Tiffany Lake, Honeymoon Pass, Whistler Pass or the Salmon Creek and Boulder Creek road system, and the eastern Pasayten file's Iron Gate, Horseshoe Basin, Chewuch and Middle Fork camps are all a long way north and west of here and serve nothing on this mountain. THE ROAD IS THE SEASON. Tiffany Springs sits at nearly six thousand eight hundred feet on gravel roads that are neither ploughed nor graded to a high standard, so this is high, dry, east-side country where the approach opens late and closes early — the couloirs melt out very soon after the roads become passable, which makes the ice line a narrow shoulder-season or winter proposition often reached on skis or a snowmobile rather than by car. AND THE 2026 FIRE PICTURE IS ON THIS MOUNTAIN, NOT NEAR IT. The Sinlahekin Fire, which passed a hundred and fifty thousand acres by mid-August 2026, had crews working directly around Tiffany Mountain extinguishing smouldering pockets in the rocky ground, with fuel reduction and line construction along Road 39 — the road to this campground. Salmon Meadows, Sugarloaf, Oriole, Kerr and Fourteen Mile campgrounds were closed and the recreation areas between Conconully and Loomis remained shut. Nothing below should be planned on until that is confirmed lifted, and expect the ground to be changed when it is.

sites.name: Tiffany Springs Campground
sites.capacity: A small primitive forest campground with a handful of sites, taking tents and modest vehicles. Trailers are not appropriate given the road. It is rarely full and it is the only organised camping anywhere near this face.
sites.water: NO POTABLE WATER AND NO TAP — this is the single most important practical fact about the place, and its name is misleading. There is no piped supply, no water service and no rubbish service. Bring everything you need for drinking, cooking and washing, or plan to treat from Tiffany Lake, which is a short walk east on the trail and is the nearest dependable open water. In late summer this whole plateau is dry and what looks like a creek on a map may be nothing at all.
sites.permit: National forest, outside designated wilderness, so there is no wilderness permit, no self-issue slip, no quota and no lottery — the opposite of the permit expectation a few miles west in the Pasayten. There is a small nightly fee at the campground and sites are first come, first served. Fire restrictions on this dry high plateau run through most of the summer and are commonly total bans, which given what has burned here recently should be treated as the default rather than the exception. Party size and stay limits are the usual forest ones.
sites.notes: This is the base for the north face and the trailhead in one, which is unusual and is what makes the face approachable at all: the walk to the bottom of the routes is under an hour, so a party can sleep at the car and still be climbing at first light without a bivouac. Trail 373 begins across the road from the campground and runs east past Tiffany Lake to Honeymoon Pass at around 7,150 ft, from where the face is below you. THE DRIVE IS THE COMMITMENT. Three ways reach it and they are not equivalent: a narrow four-wheel-drive road over Lone Frank Pass from Conconully by the North Fork Salmon Creek, about twenty miles; a longer gravel road over Baldy Pass suited to two-wheel drive, about thirty; and a good two-wheel-drive gravel line from the Methow, north out of Winthrop on the Chewuch River road and then east and north on the 37 and 39, about twenty-six miles. Road 39 itself has not been graded in some time and is not recommended for low-clearance passenger cars. At this elevation the road holds snow late into the spring and can shut with the first serious autumn storm, so the usable window is short and both ends of it are worth checking rather than assuming.

sites.name: Tiffany Lake and Little Tiffany Lake
sites.capacity: A handful of informal spots around the shores, with the established ground at the north-west end of Little Tiffany Lake. Room for a party or two. Nothing developed and no toilet, and it sees family day-hiking traffic rather than climbers.
sites.water: The lakes, and they are the dependable supply for the whole north side of this mountain — everything above them on the pass and the face runs on snowmelt and is dry once that has gone. Access to the water is easy from the trail. Treat it; these are shallow, warm, well-used lakes rather than cold alpine tarns.
sites.permit: National forest, non-wilderness. No permit, no quota, no reservation, and no fee to camp at the lakes. A pass is not required to park at the campground trailhead across the road. Fire restrictions apply through the summer and are usually total bans; carry a stove. Camp back from the shoreline on existing bare ground, and note that this trail is open to horses and mountain bikes as well as walkers, so pitch clear of it.
sites.notes: Under a mile from the campground and directly on the approach, this is the camp for a party who would rather sleep on water than at a car, or who has arrived to find the campground full or closed. It is the last certain water before the face. The trail continues around the shore and climbs about six hundred feet to Honeymoon Pass, which is the gateway to the north side; parties leaving a second vehicle at the Freezeout Ridge roadhead can carry on over Whistler Pass at around 7,600 ft to the summit and descend the Freezeout trail, an open loop of some eleven miles that is the standard way to combine the walk-up with a look at the face. THE BURN IS PART OF THE LANDSCAPE HERE. This trail travels through old fire scars that have opened the views and filled the ground with wildflower meadow, and the 2026 fire has added to that directly on this mountain — expect standing dead timber, no shade, and blowdown that changes with each windstorm. Do not pitch under dead trees in wind.

sites.name: Honeymoon Pass
sites.capacity: Open ground at the pass for a small party on gravel and thin turf. No established sites, no facilities and nothing to shelter behind. Windswept is the word most often used about this crest and it is accurate.
sites.water: None dependable. Snowmelt early in the season and nothing at all once it has gone. Everything is carried up from Tiffany Lake, six hundred feet and half a mile below, and the party that forgets this ends up walking back down for it in the evening. In the ice season it is a snow camp and you melt.
sites.permit: National forest, non-wilderness — no permit, no quota, no reservation, no fee. Fire restrictions run through the summer and there is nothing to burn at this height in any case. The turf here is thin and holds a footprint for years, so pitch on gravel or rock and leave the meadow alone.
sites.notes: The pass is where the trail crosses onto the north side and the face comes into view, and it is the tactical camp rather than the comfortable one. Its argument is a dawn start: from here the base of the routes is a short drop and a scramble rather than a walk from the road, which matters for the north-east couloir where the snow wants climbing early and matters much less for the rock, since the campground is under an hour away regardless. WHAT YOU PAY FOR THE POSITION IS WATER AND WIND, in that order, and on a face this short the trade is rarely worth it — most parties are better off sleeping at the campground or the lake and walking in. Where it does earn its keep is for a party spending two days on the face, or one continuing over Whistler Pass to the summit and out by Freezeout Ridge. Nights are cold at this elevation from late August onward and there is no shelter at all if weather comes across the plateau.

sites.name: The talus and benches below the north face
sites.capacity: No established camping. There are boulder-field benches and scraps of flat ground at the foot of the wall where one or two people could put down a bag, and nothing more — this is a place to leave packs and gear up rather than a site, and it is recorded to say so rather than to invent one.
sites.water: Snowmelt off the couloirs early, and nothing whatsoever once that has gone. Given how early the snow leaves here after the roads open, that window is short. Carry water from the lakes; there is no source at the base of the face you should plan on.
sites.permit: National forest, non-wilderness — no permit, no quota, no reservation. No fires: this is bare rock and talus with nothing to burn and fragile alpine ground around it. Standard leave-no-trace applies and human waste has to be carried out from the base of a face this small and this close to a road.
sites.notes: The routes start here and, on a face six hundred and fifty feet high forty-five minutes from a campground, essentially nobody sleeps here. It is written down because a party reading a list of camps should not be left to assume there is a bivouac at the base — there is not, and the answer to a late arrival is the campground, not the wall. THE FACE ITSELF is broken by several couloirs, aretes and vertical granite cliffs; the north-east couloir is the longest and most direct of the snow lines, on the left, and the tower at the right-hand end carries the rock routes, with the ridge line giving a vertical crack, a wide flaring chimney and long stretches of easy fourth-class scrambling on generally excellent rock. Because the snow goes soon after the roads become passable, the ice and couloir lines are a shoulder-season or winter objective and are reached by ski or snowmobile in that season rather than by driving to the campground. Treat the rock routes as the summer proposition and the couloirs as a separate trip requiring a separate approach.
